blocks.text: Functional group interconversion (FGI) means changing one functional group into another, as needed to synthesise a particular compound. FGI plays a crucial role in designing routes to target molecules: simple starting materials can be converted into more complex targets using FGIs as building blocks, and FGI helps both to create the carbon skeleton and to choose the route. The interconversions met in earlier chapters are summarised below.

blocks.alt: A map of nine boxes: alkene CH2=CH2, halogenoalkane CH3CH2Br, amine CH3CH2NH2, aldehyde CH3CHO, alcohol CH3CH2OH, amide CH3CONH2, ester CH3COOC2H5, carboxylic acid CH3COOH and acyl chloride CH3COCl, joined by labelled arrows: HBr; KOH in ethanol; NH3; KOH(aq); PBr3; steam with H3PO4; concentrated H2SO4 and heat; acidified dichromate (distil or reflux); NaBH4; LiAlH4; ethanol with H+; SOCl2; NH3 from acyl chloride to amide; LiAlH4 from amide to amine.
blocks.caption: Functional group interconversions in aliphatic compounds (original map after Figure 25.3).
blocks.long_description: Each arrow is one reaction from Chapters 21 to 24. Following the arrows shows how to get from one family to another: for example, ethene to ethanamide goes ethene -> ethanol -> ethanoic acid -> ethanoyl chloride -> ethanamide.

blocks.alt: Benzene at the centre, with arrows to methylbenzene (CH3Cl, AlCl3), benzenesulphonic acid (SO3, H2SO4), nitrobenzene (HNO3, H2SO4) and phenylethanone (CH3COCl, AlCl3). Methylbenzene goes to benzyl alcohol ((i) Cl2, light; (ii) KOH(aq)) and benzoic acid (KMnO4, H2SO4); benzenesulphonic acid to phenol ((i) NaOH; (ii) HCl); nitrobenzene to phenylamine (Sn, HCl).
blocks.caption: Functional group interconversions in aromatic compounds (original map after Figure 25.4).
blocks.long_description: Electrophilic substitution puts a new group on benzene; the new group can then be changed. Methyl groups are oxidised to COOH or chlorinated in light then hydrolysed; the sulphonic acid group is replaced by OH; the nitro group is reduced to NH2.

blocks.prompt: Why do aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition readily?
blocks.explanation: The C=O group is polar, so the carbonyl carbon is delta+ and attracts nucleophiles; its pi bond breaks easily; and the flat (trigonal) carbonyl carbon is open to attack from above or below.

blocks.prompt: How can a carboxylic acid be converted into its anhydride?
blocks.explanation: Remove water from two acid molecules with a strong dehydrating agent such as P4O10 on heating: 2CH3COOH -> (CH3CO)2O + H2O; or convert the acid into its acyl chloride (SOCl2) and react that with the sodium salt: CH3COCl + CH3COONa -> (CH3CO)2O + NaCl.
